Introducing Arete-27B: Qwen3.8-27B, post-trained to reinforce Western values.

Chinese open models are currently the strongest available, but they ship with state-aligned behavior in the weights. We built an 803-prompt eval across seven value categories, including freedom of expression, democracy, and privacy, and measured how often a model adopts China’s party line.

After fine-tuning on roughly 53 million tokens, Arete-27B's propaganda rate fell from 22% to 1%, in line with the Western models we tested. Its Hermes Bench score shows no significant performance tradeoffs.

The values in an open model are one fine-tune away. 

Our eval, weights, and training data are available now along with the full blog post: https://t.co/iAOANQTVZ6

tweets.text: And this is how you make people want to keep reading - a great example from Iain M Banks

This is the story of a man who went far away for a long time, just to play a game.

The man is a game-player called “Gurgeh.” The story starts with a battle that is not a battle, and ends with a game that is not a game.

Me?  I'll tell you about me later.

This is how the story begins…

People will talk about “storytelling” and then it’s just a bucket of loosely connected facts

Storytelling requires a story

A story has a beginning, middle, end. A protagonist, an antagonist. Maybe a loyal sidekick. A noble quest. A surprise! A pickle!! A change, a resolution.

It’s the difference between “in a galaxy far far away…” and “today we’re excited to announce that we are launching a rebel alliance”

In some stories, the protagonist is you, on your own hero’s journey

Other times, the protagonist is the customer. They have an important goal, but there’s something standing in the way. What has changed now, and why? What’s their happy ending?

x.name: alphaXiv
x.bio: High fidelity research

tweets.text:
Sparse attention reduces computation by selecting relevant tokens, but finding those tokens becomes extremely expensive at ultra-long contexts, sometimes accounting for 98% of attention's prefill time.

This paper Latent Sparse Attention (LSA) groups similar tokens into clusters and organizes them into a searchable hierarchy, letting queries to find relevant information without scanning the entire context.

At 10M tokens, LSA makes one attention layer 22.7x faster during prefill and 4.6x faster during decoding than GLM-5.3-Flash's original sparse attention, while maintaining similar accuracy.

x.bio: ceo @box - your business lives in content. unleash it with AI

tweets.text:
The interesting thing about AI agents is that as a theoretical matter, their inference can kind of run anywhere. AI is one of the few areas of technology that isn’t *as* sensitive to latency back to the user. 

Long running agents are now going to be the norm, which means it’s ok to send off work to an AI factory somewhere and that work can essentially be largely done within that remote data center and a final result spit back to the user. The data can pass into these systems in an encrypted manner, be combed through by agents, and then disregarded right after. 

And because the economic value of the task is so high relative to the latency sensitivity (eg getting back $500 in value from an automated task, but it takes an extra second to return), you don’t have to have the inference to be particularly close to the user. 

Also, because inference is a temporary process with no sensitive data needing to be stored long term where the inference is happening, you can effectively treat AI factories as ephemeral systems, changing some of the data residency dynamics slightly.

Combined, this means you have more flexibility in where you can begin to deploy AI data centers. This is both a huge economic opportunity for the states or countries (or space) that want to take advantage of this fact. And it’s a loss to the states or countries that decide to forgo the opportunity.
The future is files. And GPUs. https://t.co/fbI1NHn8u5
